preface.para: Fire is an open-source FHIR R5 server framework that generates a complete, FHIR-compliant server from a curated XML model using DSSSL code generation.

partintro.para: This part provides an overall view of the design of Fire and introduces you to key development procedures.

chapter.title: Design
chapter.para: Understanding the design of Fire is crucial for being successful in

listitem.para: deploying,
supporting,
and
using it in projects,

chapter.para: as well as for developing it further. In the following sections, the components of Fire and the design principles are documented.

sect1.title: Components
sect1.para: Fire consists of a FHIR server and the code generation infrastructure that produces it.

sect2.title: FHIR Server
sect2.para: The FHIR server is the core of Fire. It provides a standard way to access medical data. It stores data as FHIR resources and allows you to

listitem.para: query them with FHIR searches using the FHIR RESTful API,
use batch and transaction bundles to perform multiple operations atomically,
and
browse, edit, and manage resources through the built-in HTML interface.

sect2.title: Code Generator
sect2.para: The code generator produces the entire FHIR server from a curated XML model using DSSSL. This includes C# source code, SQL DDL, JavaScript, and project files.

sect1.title: Design Principles
sect1.para: The following sections describe some details of the FHIR server design such as the general data layout, data access layer, and content storage.

sect2.title: Data Model
sect2.para: For each resource type, a resource table with the resource name (e.g. Patient) exists in the public schema. A per-resource schema with the same name contains the history and search tables:

listitem.para: The main resource table. It contains one record per resource. Its fields store the ID, the current version number, and inline search parameters for non-multiple top-level properties.
This table is present only for resources with history enabled. It contains previous versions of the resource content.
Each of these tables contain search information in respect to the search parameter [name].

sect2.para: The resource content is stored as raw UTF-8 JSON bytes. For JSON responses, these bytes are written directly to the HTTP response with zero parsing and zero serialization overhead.

sect2.title: Repository Layer
sect2.para: The repository layer uses the tables in the data model implementing an API for

listitem.para: storing and loading resources,
searching for resources using the search parameters defined for them,
and
supporting functionality such as schema maintenance.

sect2.para: Currently, the repository layer supports

listitem.para: PostgreSQL,
SQL Server,
and
SQLite.

sect2.para: Most of the search parameters defined in the FHIR standard are supported.
For a given search request, a single SQL statement is built and executed, which is used for retrieving the ID/version pairs, a count value, or, in the case of autocomplete, the desired values.

If the number of search results exceeds the desired number of resources as expressed in the _count parameter (which defaults to 20 and is limited to 100), the ID/version pairs are stored in the snapshot table which supports paging through the search results.

sect2.title: Content Storage
sect2.para: Resource content is stored as raw UTF-8 JSON bytes (BYTEA in PostgreSQL, VARBINARY in SQL Server, BLOB in SQLite). For JSON responses, the bytes are written directly to the HTTP response without any parsing or serialization. Parsing to JsonNode only happens when needed for XML or HTML format conversion, bundle construction, search extraction, or composite filtering.

chapter.title: Development
chapter.para: This chapter describes working with code generation, how to build code, and producing this documentation.

sect1.title: Generating Code
sect1.para: The entire code of the FHIR server is generated from an XML model which is, in turn, obtained from the FHIR specification. The following sections provide an overview of this process.

sect2.title: Design
sect2.para: The FHIR server is built by performing the following steps:

listitem.para: Processing the JSON files from the Downloads page of the FHIR specification using the Modeler,
Editing the obtained fhir.xml by commenting out unsupported parts and adding non-standard features.
Generating code from fhir.xml.

sect2.title: The Modeler
sect2.para: The FHIR specification is formulated in a set of resources like StructureDefinition, OperationDefinition, CodeSystem, ValueSet, and SearchParameter.
These following JSON files from the zip file are read and processed:

listitem.para: The resources.
The data types.
The value sets and code systems.
The search parameters.

sect2.para: The Modeler reads all information required for code generation from these files, fixes some structural problems and inconsistencies, and consolidates it into one XML file fhir.xml.

sect2.title: Editing the XML Model
sect2.para: The fhir.xml output of the Modeler contains all resources and search parameters from the FHIR specification. Resources are activated for code generation by setting their active attribute to true.
The following elements and attributes are defined in the fhirspec.dtd (with the obvious plural elements and the id and name attributes omitted):

listitem.para: A resource definition. The active attribute shows whether the FHIR server shall support the resource. The history attribute controls whether versioning is enabled for the resource.
A description of a resource, element, property, codeset, codeset, code, operation, or parameter to be used as inline code documentation comments or for producing reference documentation content.
The definition of a data type, either global or in the scope of a resource. The backbone attribute is true if the element is a BackboneType, i.e, if it contains the modifierExtension property.

A property of a resource or an element. The iscollection attribute is true if the multiplicity of the property can be greater than 1. The notnull attribute is true if its multiplicity must be at least 1. The summary attribute is true if the property is included in resource summaries.The summary attribute is true if the property is a modifier.

A possible data type of a property. The type attribute refers to its data type. The default is string. The ref attribute links to an element if the type is element. If the type is code and the ref attribute is present, then it links to a codeset element which contains the possible codes for a code property with the Required binding strength.
A possible target resource type of a reference variant.

A set of possible codes. The type attribute refers to its data type. The default is string. The ref attribute links to an element if the type is element. If the type is code and the ref attribute is present, then it links to a codeset element which contains the possible codes.
A possible code with the value attribute as its value.

A description of a search parameter. The query attribute is an alternative name of the search parameter to be used in programming languages like C. The type attribute is the search parameter type. The customsort attribute is true for a search parameter with custom sorting behavior.
A possible path for a search parameter.

A part of a search path. The ref attribute links to the property that represents this search path part. The resolve attribute links to a variant of the property which is to be used for this part. The property and type attributes may impose a condition on this part. The first attribute means that only the first element of this part is considered for matching. The notnull attribute means that the part must not be null for being considered for matching. The variant, op, and value attributes select names a variant, an operation, and a value to be used as matching criterion.
A possible variant of a search path. The to attribute of this element links to a possible variant of a search path or a component of a composite search parameter .
A component of a composite search parameter. The ref attribute of this element links to the property for this component.

sect2.title: The Code Generator
sect2.para: The entire FHIR server is generated from fhir.xml using Dazzle, a DSSSL processor. DSSSL is the Document Style Semantics and Specification Language. Much valuable information about DSSSL processors can be found on the home page of Jade. Generating both the code and the documentation of the FHIR server relies heavily on the non-standard SGML Transformation backend.
Code is generated by running the fire.sh script in the git repository root. This script runs Dazzle with codegen/map.dsl as the main stylesheet.
The code generation is controlled by on/off switches in codegen/config.scm and produces the following output:

listitem.para: Generated by codegen/boilerplate.scm: the project file, Program.cs, Database.cs, and cross-resource helpers like SearchHelper, BundleHandler, and FhirXmlSerializer.
Generated by codegen/migration.scm: database schemas, resource tables, history tables, and search index tables for all three database backends.
Generated by codegen/models.scm: per-resource model classes with search extraction methods.
Generated by codegen/repositories.scm: per-resource CRUD and search with parameterized SQL.
Generated by codegen/handlers.scm: per-resource minimal API handlers with enum validation and FHIR HTTP semantics.
Generated by codegen/js.scm: per-resource browser-based resource editing UI.
Generated by codegen/html.scm: per-resource reference documentation pages and the resource list page.

sect1.title: Producing Documentation
sect1.para: The Fire documentation is accessible via the index.html page of the FHIR server. This section describes how to write the documentation source, and how to generate the documentation HTML files.

sect2.title: Writing
sect2.para: The prose parts of the documentation are written in DocBook, an XML documentation schema especially well suited for describing hardware and software. Currently, one single source file documentation/fire.xml contains the complete prose contents of the documentation.
The reference parts like the reference pages of the individual resources are generated from fhir.xml along with the code of the FHIR server.

The file fire.xml can be edited using any text editor. Working on this file with an XML editor should be more convenient. Visual Studio Code with a good XML extension can aid you with the writing by proposing or closing elements and indicating XML structure errors.

sect2.title: Generating Documentation
sect2.para: You generate the prose parts of the documentation by running the docu.sh script in the git repository root. This command runs Dazzle which uses codegen/documentation.dsl for transforming the DocBook contents of fire.xml into HTML.

partintro.para: This part gives an overview over planning a Fire installation, deploying it, and maintenance tasks like creating and dropping schemas, and browsing, deleting, and editing data.

chapter.title: Planning
chapter.para: Planning for a Fire installation involves making decisions about

listitem.para: the operating system,
the database technology,
and
the processor architecture.

sect1.title: Operating System
sect1.para: Since Fire runs on .NET, it can in principle run on any operating system supported by the .NET platform. Popular choices are

listitem.para: Linux,
Windows,
and
macOS.

sect2.title: Linux
sect2.para: Running Fire on Linux in a Docker based installation is recommended for its ease of installation and maintenance.

Since Docker completely isolates the server from the hosting operating system (which can be itself be virtualized), you can run Fire either on premises or in cloud-based services like Amazon Web Services or Microsoft Azure.

sect2.title: Windows
sect2.para: Running Fire on Windows can be useful

listitem.para: for local deployment during development,
or
for on-premises or cloud-based installations for organizations with limited experience with Linux or Docker.

sect2.title: Mac OS
sect2.para: For local development, you can use any editor or IDE to develop Fire.
For offline work if internet access is not available, you can use Docker Desktop to run PostgreSQL as a local database server. Alternatively, SQLite can be used without any external database server.

sect1.title: Processor Architecture
sect1.para: For many years, processors with the Intel 64 bit architecture, made by Intel or AMD, were the obvious choice for running server software in general.
In the last years, processors with ARM architecture have become available with the major cloud providers, and are now used in desktop and laptop computers as well.

sect2.title: Intel
sect2.para: For decades, using processors with the Intel 64 bit architecture was a no-brainer because of their maturity and ubiquitous availability.

The design of these processors, however, carries a heavy burden of a complex instruction set that dates back to the seventies of the last century, when it was originally designed for a 16-bit processor. The instruction set has then been extended for 32-bit and finally 64-bit processors. The basic structure of the instruction set, however, remained unchanged. Modern processors of this type have to translate the instructions internally to execute them which causes massive overhead in terms of power consumption for a certain workload.
Therefore, you should consider running and even developing Fire on an ARM based platform.

sect2.title: ARM
sect2.para: The big advantage of the ARM architecture is a much lower power consumption which helps reducing your energy costs and your carbon footprint. In cloud environments, this should directly relate to lower prices for the same workload.
You can run Fire on ARM based cloud instances like AWS Graviton EC2 instances.
It makes even sense to do Fire development on an ARM based MacBook because compiling on such a machine drains the battery much slower.

sect1.title: Database
sect1.para: Fire stores FHIR resources in a relational database which can be

listitem.para: PostgreSQL,
SQL Server,
or
SQLite.

sect1.para: The decision for one or the other technology depends on the requirements of the deployment environment and the availability of database administration know-how in the organization.

sect2.title: PostgreSQL
sect2.para: Using PostgreSQL is the primary option for storing the FHIR resources. It is the most thoroughly tested database backend.
Even though PostgreSQL requires very little database administration work, it is important to perform database backups on a regular basis.

sect2.title: MS SQL Server
sect2.para: If your organization has specialized SQL Server administration know-how, you may consider using SQL Server for storing the FHIR resources. SQL Server is a very mature database platform with many monitoring and optimization options.

sect2.title: SQLite
sect2.para: SQLite is useful for development, testing, and small-scale deployments where running a separate database server is not desired. It requires no installation or configuration.

chapter.title: Deployment
chapter.para: Deploying Fire is possible as a Docker container or, on Windows, as a Windows service.

sect1.title: Docker
sect1.para: Fire can be deployed as a Docker container.
Adjust the settings in the appsettings.json file.

sect1.title: Windows
sect1.para: Fire can be deployed as a Windows service.
To install Fire as a Windows service, perform the following steps:

listitem.para: Build the project with
Copy the binaries from the bin\Release\net10.0\publish directory to a directory on your computer.
Log into a command prompt with Administrator rights.
Run the sc create for the service to be created. An example:
The space after the binPath= is important. If you omit it, the command will not work.
Adjust the settings in the appsettings.json file in the directory of the service.

sect1.title: Configuring
sect1.para: The appsettings.json file contains the following parameters which have to be configured for your installation:

listitem.para: PostgreSql, SqlServer, or Sqlite, depending on your database type.
The connection string to your database.
The URLs that are allowed for cross-origin access.
The key required for administrative operations such as index management, purging deleted data, and managing search tables.
Optional path to a directory containing FHIR resource JSON files to be loaded as seed data on startup.

chapter.title: Maintenance
chapter.para: This chapter describes database schema management, and browsing, editing, and deleting data with just the FHIR server itself.

sect1.title: Database Schemas
sect1.para: Fire automatically creates all database schemas, tables, and indices when the server starts. There is no manual schema creation step required. Simply create an empty database according to the connection string in the configuration file and start the server.
If a software update introduces new resources or search parameters, the server will create the necessary tables and indices on the next startup.
In a development or testing environment, you can reset the database by dropping and recreating it, then restarting the server.

sect2.title: Managing Indexes
sect2.para: Fire provides administrative endpoints for managing search indexes. These endpoints require the PurgeKey for authorization.
To create all search indexes:
Example: /admin/indexes/create/c522382c-8656-463e-8277-b913e4466f53
To drop all search indexes:
Example: /admin/indexes/drop/c522382c-8656-463e-8277-b913e4466f53

sect2.title: Managing Search Tables
sect2.para: If a software update introduces new search parameters, the following endpoints allow you to create or drop individual search tables. These endpoints require the PurgeKey for authorization.
To create a search table and populate it with index data from all existing resources:
Example: /admin/createsearch/Patient/family/c522382c-8656-463e-8277-b913e4466f53
To drop a search table:
Example: /admin/dropsearch/Patient/family/c522382c-8656-463e-8277-b913e4466f53

sect2.title: Purging Deleted Data
sect2.para: When resources are deleted, their history records are retained in the resource_history table. To permanently remove all history records of deleted resources:
Example: /purgeschema/Patient/c522382c-8656-463e-8277-b913e4466f53

sect2.title: Rolling Back to a Previous Version
sect2.para: For resources with history enabled, you can roll back to a previous version. This restores the content of the specified version as the current version of the resource:

sect2.title: Undeleting Deleted Data
sect2.para: When a resource is deleted by a DELETE request, Fire copies the record to the resource_history table with a DELETE marker and removes it from the resource table. You can still access the history of the deleted resource with FHIR's history interaction.
To undelete a single resource:
To undelete all deleted resources of a certain resource type:
Example: /admin/undelete/Patient/c522382c-8656-463e-8277-b913e4466f53
The response includes the number of restored resources, for example: {"restored": 5}.

sect2.title: Seeding Data

sect1.title: Browsing and Deleting Data
sect1.para: With Fire, you can browse, edit, create, and delete any resource without the need for a front-end app. This is especially useful for inspecting data or for resource types not yet supported by any app.

To get started, simply enter any legal FHIR search URL in the browser URL field to get a bundle page formatted as a table, or a simple resource read URI to get directly to the resource page for the requested resource in an editable format.

sect2.title: Bundle Page
sect2.para: If you enter a valid FHIR search URL in your browser URL input field, such as

(replacing myhost by the host name of your actual FHIR server, and the port if applicable), the browser will send that search request to your FHIR server, receive a bundle of resources and display that bundle in a table format.
This bundle page lets you

listitem.para: delete selected resources or all of the resources which match the search that you have entered in the URL field of the browser,
download the results of the search as a JSON bundle file,
browse the snapshot using navigation links if applicable,
and
clicking on the resource link in a line of the table to navigate to that resource.

sect2.title: Resource Page
sect2.para: The resource page allows you to

listitem.para: inspect and edit the contents of a resource,
navigate to resources which are referenced,
and
navigate to resources which reference the current resource.

sect2.para: To navigate to a referenced resource, click the link in the editing area of the resource.
To download the current resource as a JSON file, click Download JSON.
To display the versions of the current resource, click History.

Below the editing area of the resources, there is the navigation area which allows you to load resources which reference the current resource. Each line in the navigation area contain links for each reference search parameter for a certain resource type that targets the current resource. Click on a link to perform the search for all resources of that type which reference the current resource.

sect1.title: Editing Resources
sect1.para: To edit and save a resource, perform one or more of the following steps:

listitem.para: To add an element, click the + button next to the name of the field and enter the data in the field.
To remove an element, click the - button.
To edit a resource reference, select edit in the drop-down list before the link and edit the reference. To display the reference as a link, select link. To remove the reference, select -.
To save the changed contents of the resource, click Save.

sect1.para: To create a new resource, perform the following steps:

listitem.para: Click New.
Enter the data of the new resource.
To save the resource, click Save.

sect1.para: To delete the current version of a resource, perform the following steps:

listitem.para: Click Rollback.
Click Ok.

sect2.title: Limitations
sect2.para: Known limitations of the search:

listitem.para: The search parameter phonetic (Patient, Practitioner and every other resource with a name) does no phonetic matching. It is indexed and answered exactly like name: a case-insensitive match on the beginning of any part of the name. A search for phonetic=Meier finds what name=Meier finds, and does not find Mayer or Maier.

sect2.title: Autocomplete
sect2.para: Each resource type exposes a GET /fire/{Resource}/$autocomplete operation that returns matching values from search index tables as a plain JSON string array. The query string uses the same format as regular FHIR search — a working search URL can be converted to autocomplete by inserting $autocomplete into the path.

formalpara.title: Examples
formalpara.para: Search for patient names starting with "smi": /fire/Patient/$autocomplete?name=smi

sect2.para: Use _count and _offset to limit results: /fire/Patient/$autocomplete?name=smi&_count=5
Look up values for a specific resource by ID. The HTML UI uses this to resolve references to human-readable names: /fire/Patient/$autocomplete?_id=123&_autocomplete=name

formalpara.title: Response Format
formalpara.para: Returns a plain JSON string array:

formalpara.title: Supported Search Parameters
formalpara.para: The search parameter and _autocomplete can be _id, any string search parameter (e.g. name, family, given), or non-inline token search parameter (e.g. identifier). Inline search parameters (those stored directly on the resource table rather than in a separate search index table) are not available for autocomplete.

listitem.para: Which search parameter's values to return. Defaults to the search parameter. Specify only when different, e.g. _autocomplete=family.
Maximum number of results. If omitted, all results are returned.
Number of results to skip. Defaults to 0.
